questions.question: What are the four cloud deployment models?
questions.answer: Public Cloud (owned by providers like AWS, shared across customers), Private Cloud (dedicated to one organization), Hybrid Cloud (combination of public and private), and Community Cloud (shared among organizations with similar compliance needs). The most common in enterprise environments are Public and Hybrid.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Data Center and the Cloud?
questions.answer: A data center is a physical building containing servers, storage, and networking equipment. The cloud is a delivery model — on-demand, scalable, automated, pay-as-you-go access to computing resources. A private cloud can live inside a data center, but uses cloud-like automation (VMware, OpenStack) on top of dedicated physical infrastructure.

questions.question: Explain IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS with examples.
questions.answer: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) provides raw infrastructure — servers, storage, networking. AWS example: EC2. You manage the OS and above. PaaS (Platform as a Service) adds a runtime platform — you deploy code only. AWS example: Elastic Beanstalk, Lambda. SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers fully managed applications. Example: Gmail, Zoom, AWS WorkMail. Memory trick: IaaS = you manage most. PaaS = you just code. SaaS = you just use.

questions.question: What is the AWS Shared Responsibility Model?
questions.answer: It defines what AWS secures versus what the customer secures. AWS is responsible for security 'of' the cloud — physical data centers, hardware, networking, and the hypervisor. The customer is responsible for security 'in' the cloud — their data, IAM configurations, OS patching (for IaaS), application code, and network settings like security groups. The more managed the service, the more responsibility shifts to AWS.

questions.question: What is virtualization and why is it fundamental to cloud computing?
questions.answer: Virtualization is technology that allows multiple virtual machines to run on a single physical server by abstracting hardware through a hypervisor. It enables cloud providers to serve thousands of customers from the same physical infrastructure through multi-tenancy, provide rapid scalability (spin up a VM in seconds), ensure isolation between customer workloads, and dramatically reduce cost by eliminating the 1:1 server-to-customer ratio.

questions.question: What is a hypervisor? What are the two types?
questions.answer: A hypervisor is software that sits between physical hardware and virtual machines, allocating CPU, RAM, and storage to each VM and enforcing isolation. Type 1 (bare-metal) runs directly on hardware — no host OS needed. Examples: VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, AWS Nitro. Faster, more efficient, used in production and cloud. Type 2 (hosted) runs on top of an existing OS. Examples: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation. Used for development and testing on personal computers.

questions.question: What is the AWS Nitro System?
questions.answer: The AWS Nitro System is AWS's custom Type 1 bare-metal hypervisor. Instead of running virtualization in software (which consumes CPU), Nitro offloads virtualization, networking, and storage functions to dedicated Nitro hardware cards. This delivers near bare-metal performance for EC2 instances and reduces the hypervisor attack surface — important for customer isolation and security.

questions.question: What are three advantages and three disadvantages of virtualization?
questions.answer: Advantages: (1) Efficient resource utilization — multiple VMs share hardware with no waste. (2) Cost savings — fewer physical servers, lower power and maintenance costs. (3) Isolation — a VM crash or attack doesn't affect other VMs on the same host. Disadvantages: (1) Performance overhead — VMs are slower than bare-metal due to the hypervisor layer. (2) Single point of failure — if the physical host fails, all VMs go down. (3) Resource contention (noisy neighbor) — too many VMs fighting for CPU/RAM degrades performance.

questions.question: What are the four types of virtualization used in cloud computing?
questions.answer: (1) Server Virtualization — multiple VMs on one physical server. AWS: EC2. (2) Storage Virtualization — pooling physical storage into one virtual storage system. AWS: EBS, S3. (3) Network Virtualization — virtual networks on shared hardware. AWS: VPC. (4) Desktop Virtualization — remote virtual desktops. AWS: WorkSpaces.

questions.question: How does the Shared Responsibility Model change for IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS?
questions.answer: For IaaS (EC2): AWS manages hardware and hypervisor; customer manages OS, runtime, app, data. For PaaS (Elastic Beanstalk): AWS takes on OS and runtime too; customer manages only app code and data. For SaaS (WorkMail): AWS manages everything; customer only manages their own data and user access. As the service becomes more managed, AWS takes on more responsibility and the customer takes on less.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to choose between a managed and unmanaged cloud service.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team needed to deploy a Node.js web application on AWS with limited DevOps resources. (Task) Decide between EC2 (IaaS — we manage the OS) or Elastic Beanstalk (PaaS — AWS manages infrastructure). (Action) Chose Elastic Beanstalk because our team had two developers with no dedicated sysadmin — we couldn't commit time to OS patching, scaling configuration, and load balancer setup. (Result) Deployment time dropped from estimated 2 weeks of setup to 2 days, and auto-scaling handled traffic spikes without any manual intervention. The trade-off was less OS-level control, which was acceptable for this workload.

questions.question: Describe a scenario where you would recommend Private Cloud over Public Cloud.
questions.answer: (Situation) A client in healthcare needed to store and process patient medical records. (Task) Recommend a cloud deployment model that met HIPAA compliance requirements and internal data sovereignty policies. (Action) Recommended a private cloud built on VMware in their existing data center — this gave them dedicated infrastructure under their control, meeting compliance requirements that prevented data from residing on shared multi-tenant infrastructure. (Result) Client achieved cloud-like automation and self-service for internal teams while maintaining full data control required by their compliance team. We noted future migration to AWS GovCloud as a path if they wanted public cloud benefits with compliance guarantees.

questions.question: A customer reports their EC2 instance was breached via a weak SSH password. Who is responsible and what should be done?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 instance compromised via weak OS-level SSH credentials. (Task) Identify responsibility and remediation path. (Action) This is entirely the customer's responsibility under the Shared Responsibility Model — SSH access credentials are 'in the cloud' (customer-managed). AWS is not responsible for customer-configured passwords or key pair management. Immediate steps: terminate the compromised instance, launch a new instance with a strong key pair, restrict SSH access to specific IP ranges via Security Groups, and enable AWS CloudTrail for audit logging. (Result) Security restored. Going forward, recommended disabling SSH password authentication entirely and using key pairs only.

questions.question: A startup says 'we need full OS access and the ability to install custom kernel modules.' What AWS service do you recommend and why?
questions.answer: (Situation) Startup needs proprietary driver installation and custom kernel module support. (Task) Identify the right AWS compute service and cloud model. (Action) Recommended Amazon EC2 (IaaS). PaaS options like Elastic Beanstalk or Lambda abstract away the OS — you cannot install custom kernel modules when you don't control the OS layer. EC2 with a custom AMI gives full OS access and allows any kernel configuration. (Result) Customer launched a custom AMI with their kernel modules pre-installed, deployed it across their EC2 fleet using Auto Scaling.

questions.question: How would you explain the difference between a Data Center and the Cloud to a non-technical executive?
questions.answer: (Situation) CTO asked me to brief the board on a proposed cloud migration. (Task) Explain the technical distinction clearly. (Action) Used the house analogy: 'Building a data center is like buying land and constructing a house — large upfront investment, you own it completely, but you're responsible for all maintenance, repairs, and you've committed to that fixed space forever. The cloud is like renting an apartment in a premium building — you move in today, pay monthly, scale to a bigger apartment if you grow, and the building handles plumbing and electricity. Our data center is the land. AWS is the apartment building.' (Result) Board approved cloud migration budget, understanding OpEx vs. CapEx implications clearly.

questions.question: A company asks: 'We're on EC2 today. If we move to RDS for our database, do we still need to patch the database engine?' Answer this using the Shared Responsibility Model.
questions.answer: (Situation) Company migrating from self-managed MySQL on EC2 to Amazon RDS. (Task) Clarify responsibility shift for database patching. (Action) Explained the model shift: On EC2 (IaaS), the customer is fully responsible for MySQL installation, configuration, and patching — it's their OS and their database. On RDS (managed PaaS), AWS takes over database engine patching, OS patching, hardware management, and high availability. The customer retains responsibility for database access control (Security Groups, IAM), data encryption settings, backup retention periods, and query performance tuning. (Result) Team reduced database administration overhead by ~60% while maintaining control over security and performance settings.

questions.question: Describe the 'noisy neighbor' problem in virtualization and how it affects cloud performance.
questions.answer: (Situation) Customer reported intermittent performance degradation on their EC2 instances during peak hours. (Task) Investigate and explain potential cause. (Action) Explained resource contention: multiple VMs on the same physical host compete for CPU, RAM, and disk I/O. If one VM runs an intensive workload, other VMs on the same host may experience slower performance — the 'noisy neighbor' effect. Recommended moving to EC2 Dedicated Instances or Dedicated Hosts, which ensure the physical hardware is not shared with other AWS customers. (Result) Performance issues resolved. Also noted that AWS Nitro's hardware offload architecture reduces contention by handling network and storage virtualization in dedicated hardware, not shared CPU.

questions.question: A security audit flags that your team hasn't been patching the OS on your EC2 instances for 3 months. How do you address this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Security audit found EC2 OS patches 3 months behind. (Task) Remediate and prevent recurrence. (Action) Immediate: Used AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager to assess patch compliance across all instances and apply critical patches. Scheduled a maintenance window for non-critical patches. Long-term: Set up automatic patching via SSM Patch Manager with weekly scan + patch schedule. Considered migrating suitable workloads to Elastic Beanstalk or ECS/Fargate (PaaS/container), where AWS handles OS patching entirely. (Result) All critical patches applied within 24 hours. Ongoing patching automated — audit findings resolved. Key lesson: OS patching on EC2 is always the customer's responsibility under the Shared Responsibility Model.

questions.question: How does the Shared Responsibility Model change your approach to security when migrating from on-premises to AWS?
questions.answer: On-premises, you're responsible for everything: physical security, hardware, networking, OS, application, and data. On AWS, the model splits this. You no longer worry about physical data center security, hardware failures, or network infrastructure — AWS handles those. But you gain new responsibilities specific to cloud: IAM policy design, security group configuration, encryption settings that must be explicitly enabled, CloudTrail logging, and understanding which services manage their own OS vs. requiring customer patches. The risk isn't less — it's different. Cloud security failures are predominantly misconfiguration (wrong IAM policies, open S3 buckets), not infrastructure failures.

questions.question: Design a hybrid cloud architecture for a financial institution that needs regulatory compliance for transaction data but wants cloud scalability for its mobile banking app.
questions.answer: Architecture: Private cloud (VMware in on-premises data center) for transaction processing, core banking system, and customer financial records — meets PCI-DSS and regulatory data residency requirements. AWS public cloud for mobile banking app backend (EC2/EBS), API Gateway, authentication services, and analytics dashboards. AWS Direct Connect provides a private, dedicated network link between on-premises and AWS — encrypted, not over the public internet, meeting compliance requirements for data in transit. AWS Security Hub and CloudTrail deployed in the public cloud component for compliance monitoring. Shared responsibility: on-premises systems are fully the institution's responsibility; AWS components follow the standard model. Key benefit: core transaction data never leaves the private cloud, but the customer-facing app scales elastically on AWS.

questions.question: What architectural decisions would you make differently using IaaS vs. PaaS for a microservices application?
questions.answer: With IaaS (EC2): you control OS, runtime version, network configuration, and can install any dependency. Better for workloads needing specific kernel features, custom runtimes, or legacy dependencies. Downside: you own patching, scaling configuration, load balancer setup. With PaaS (Elastic Beanstalk, ECS Fargate, Lambda): faster deployment, auto-scaling built in, no OS management. Better for stateless microservices with standard runtimes. Architectural differences: IaaS uses EC2 + ALB + Auto Scaling Groups (you wire these together). PaaS/containers use Fargate + ECS Service (AWS manages the runtime layer). For greenfield microservices with no unusual dependencies — default to containers (PaaS-like). For legacy lift-and-shift or custom OS needs — IaaS on EC2.

questions.question: How does the AWS Nitro System solve the performance overhead problem traditionally associated with virtualization?
questions.answer: Traditional software hypervisors (like Xen or KVM running in software) consume a portion of host CPU cycles to handle virtualization tasks: emulating network interfaces, managing storage I/O, enforcing isolation. This creates overhead — VMs get less raw CPU than a bare-metal server. AWS Nitro offloads these functions to dedicated Nitro hardware cards: the Nitro Card for VPC networking, the Nitro Card for EBS storage, and the Nitro Security Chip. The host CPU is entirely freed for customer workloads. Result: EC2 instances get near bare-metal CPU performance. Additionally, by moving hypervisor logic into purpose-built hardware with minimal attack surface, Nitro significantly reduces the risk of hypervisor vulnerabilities compared to complex software hypervisors.

questions.question: A company wants to adopt the cloud but their compliance team says 'customer data must never reside on shared hardware.' Is this compatible with public cloud, and how would you address it?
questions.answer: This is a common compliance requirement. In standard public cloud, customer VMs share physical hardware (multi-tenancy via virtualization). The solution within AWS: EC2 Dedicated Hosts or Dedicated Instances. A Dedicated Host gives a physical AWS server exclusively to one customer — no other customer's VMs run on it. Dedicated Instances ensure instances run on hardware dedicated to that account. Both options eliminate shared physical hardware while retaining public cloud benefits (managed infrastructure, global reach, pay-as-you-go). Cost is higher than standard instances. Alternative: evaluate whether the compliance requirement is truly about physical hardware isolation or just logical isolation — for most modern compliance frameworks, AWS's virtualization isolation is legally sufficient and compliance teams can be satisfied with AWS's compliance certifications (SOC 2, PCI-DSS, HIPAA BAA).

questions.question: Explain why the Shared Responsibility Model means that 'moving to AWS doesn't automatically make you more secure.'
questions.answer: The Shared Responsibility Model clarifies that AWS secures the physical infrastructure — but everything the customer deploys and configures remains their responsibility. The most common cloud security failures are not AWS infrastructure failures — they are customer misconfiguration: open S3 bucket permissions exposing sensitive data, overly permissive IAM policies allowing privilege escalation, EC2 security groups with 0.0.0.0/0 ingress on port 22, unencrypted databases (RDS encryption must be explicitly enabled), and no MFA on root accounts. AWS provides the tools: KMS, IAM, Security Groups, CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Security Hub — but you must use them. Moving to AWS gives you better tools and removes infrastructure security burden, but does not automatically configure security for your workloads. Security posture depends on how well you apply the Shared Responsibility Model.

questions.question: How would you architect a disaster recovery solution for a virtualized on-premises environment using AWS, leveraging VM snapshot concepts?
questions.answer: Disaster recovery architecture using AWS: On-premises VMs (VMware) are replicated to AWS using AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) or AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS). These services continuously replicate server data to AWS — maintaining a low-RPO (recovery point objective) copy. DRS monitors replication health and can recover servers in minutes. In a disaster event: trigger failover in DRS — AWS launches EC2 instances from the replicated snapshots (similar to VM snapshots) in a pre-configured VPC. Recovery time objective (RTO) drops from hours (hardware procurement) to minutes (VM launch). Cost model: storage costs only during standby; compute costs only during DR test or failover. This architecture demonstrates the practical application of VM snapshot/replication concepts from this session — applied at enterprise scale for business continuity.
